screens.title: Why a holistic approach matters
screens.narratorSegment: Hybrid environments introduce two domains of visibility: the cloud provider's telemetry and your on-premises telemetry. A holistic approach recognizes that neither side alone gives full context. CloudWatch provides precise metrics for AWS-managed components — tunnel states, connection throughput, BGP session state — but it cannot see inside your customer gateway device, your internal routing, or your ISP's network. For example, a VPN tunnel metric flipping to DOWN may show the symptom, but the root cause is often an on-premises internet outage or a router interface failure. To avoid a lengthy process of elimination, proactively collect CGW logs, interface counters, C P U and memory metrics on the device, and ISP health indicators. Then correlate those with CloudWatch metrics in a single incident management workflow. Practically, this means creating alarms for key CloudWatch metrics, enriching alerts with on-prem alert data, and documenting runbooks that specify which on-prem data to check first. A common misconception is that CloudWatch alarms alone are sufficient: they are necessary but not sufficient. The core takeaway is that fast diagnosis requires correlated signals from both sides so you can distinguish provider-side faults from customer-side failures without guesswork.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Holistic monitoring
Core Concept

Why a holistic approach matters

Cloud-side metrics show symptoms; on-premises telemetry often shows root cause. Both are required for fast repair.

Key signals to correlate:
  • TunnelState and VPNConnectionState from CloudWatch.
  • CGW interface status, CPU, and logs from your device monitoring.
  • ISP outage or packet loss indicators for VPNs.
Key Takeaway

End-to-end visibility means correlating CloudWatch metrics with local device telemetry before escalating to providers or opening tickets.

Annotated scenario
Cloud symptom
TunnelState toggles between UP and DOWN for tunnel 1.
On-prem evidence
CGW logs show interface flaps and ISP packet loss at the same timestamps.
Action
Correlate times, raise ISP ticket, and failover traffic to second tunnel if available.
Common mistake: Relying solely on aggregate metrics like VPNConnectionState without inspecting per-tunnel TunnelState or device logs.

screens.title: Site-to-Site VPN: key CloudWatch metrics
screens.narratorSegment: AWS exposes several metrics that describe the state and throughput of Site-to-Site VPN connections. The most crucial metric for operational alerts is TunnelState: it is binary and tells you whether an individual tunnel is UP or DOWN. Because VPN connections usually have two redundant tunnels, monitoring TunnelState per tunnel avoids missing a single-tunnel failure. TunnelDataIn and TunnelDataOut measure bytes flowing through each tunnel; these are useful for spotting traffic drops, bottlenecks, or skew in active/active setups. Use TunnelData metrics to verify traffic is balanced when you expect it to be, and to detect sudden volume changes that may indicate an outage on one path. VPNConnectionState gives an aggregated view for the whole connection — helpful for dashboards but too coarse for rapid troubleshooting. Finally, newer metric names like IPSecTunnelState provide more detailed phase status for IPSec negotiations. A common misconception is treating VPNConnectionState as sufficient; it can hide single-tunnel failures. The practical rule is: alert on TunnelState for each tunnel, review TunnelData counters for performance issues, and use the aggregate metric for high-level dashboards. This combination gives both speed and context during incidents.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › VPN Metrics
Definition

Site-to-Site VPN metrics

Metrics provide per-tunnel and per-connection visibility. Use each for a specific purpose.

TunnelState
Binary per-tunnel status (1 = UP, 0 = DOWN). Critical for immediate alerts.
TunnelDataIn / TunnelDataOut
Bytes in/out per tunnel. Used for traffic patterns and load balancing checks.
VPNConnectionState / IPSecTunnelState
Aggregated or IPSec-phase details for higher-level views or deep diagnostics.
Example
Symptom
Tunnel 0 TunnelState oscillates between 1 and 0; Tunnel 1 remains 1.
Likely cause
On-premise internet instability or CGW interface flapping for the affected tunnel.
Key Takeaway

Per-tunnel metrics are essential. Use TunnelState for alerts and TunnelData counters for performance insights.

screens.title: Responding to a TunnelState alarm
screens.narratorSegment: When a TunnelState alarm fires, follow a concise, stepwise process to isolate the fault domain quickly. First, confirm the alarm's timestamp and whether only one tunnel or both tunnels are affected. If only one tunnel is down, your first check should be the on-premises customer gateway device: review interface up/down events, C P U, memory, and the device logs for any IPSec negotiation errors. Second, check the internet path between your facility and AWS, looking for ISP outages or increased packet loss that could explain intermittent tunnel failures. Third, on the AWS side examine the tunnel's CloudWatch metrics and VPN console details to verify configuration values such as tunnel IP address and IPSec parameters. Fourth, if BGP is in use, check that session state has not been affected; a tunnel that is UP but with BGP down will still block routes. Finally, escalate to the appropriate partner — ISP, hardware vendor, or AWS Support — with correlated timestamps and logs. A common mistake is assuming the cloud side is always the problem; in practice, one tunnel failing while the redundant tunnel remains healthy usually indicates a customer-side path or device issue. This checklist reduces guesswork and speeds resolution.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › TunnelState Response
Process Flow

Responding to a TunnelState alarm

  1. Confirm alarm time and which tunnel(s) are affected.
  2. Inspect customer gateway device logs and interface counters for flaps or resource exhaustion.
  3. Check ISP path health and packet loss during the event window.
  4. Validate AWS VPN configuration and CloudWatch tunnel metrics for mismatches.
  5. Verify BGP session state if routing issues persist, then escalate with correlated logs.
Example scenario
Observed
Tunnel 0 TunnelState = 0 at 10:12, Tunnel 1 = 1. CGW log shows interface down at 10:11.
Action taken
Contact ISP with timestamps and failover traffic to the healthy tunnel until the CGW interface is repaired.
Pro-tip: Always attach CGW logs and ISP timestamps to your escalation to avoid back-and-forth evidence requests.

screens.title: Direct Connect metrics and BGP
screens.narratorSegment: Direct Connect provides a dedicated physical link between your premises and AWS. Because it bypasses the public internet, monitoring focuses on physical link health and routing. ConnectionState tells you whether the Direct Connect link is UP or DOWN — analogous to a physical port or circuit status. ConnectionBpsIngress and ConnectionBpsEgress show bandwidth utilization in bits per second and are essential for capacity planning and detecting saturation. ConnectionErrorCount counts physical layer errors; a rising error count can indicate cabling or port issues and should trigger hardware-level investigations. Critically, BGPState is the metric that reports the status of the Border Gateway Protocol session for each virtual interface. A common operational trap is assuming a UP link guarantees traffic flow; if ConnectionState is UP but BGPState is DOWN, routes are not exchanged and traffic will not be forwarded. For this reason, alerts on BGPState should be treated as high priority even when the physical connection appears healthy. Practical monitoring combines link health, bandwidth, error counts, and BGP session state into a single operational view so that you can decide quickly between hardware, configuration, or routing problems.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Direct Connect Metrics
Definition

Direct Connect metrics

ConnectionState: UP/DOWN for the physical link.
ConnectionBpsIngress/Egress: Bandwidth utilization for capacity and saturation checks.
ConnectionErrorCount: Physical errors indicating cabling or port faults.
BGPState: The routing session state for each virtual interface; critical for route exchange.
Scenario
Observed
ConnectionState = 1, but users cannot reach VPC resources.
Likely cause
BGPState is DOWN; routes are not exchanged despite the link being up.
Common mistake: Alerting only on ConnectionState and ignoring BGPState, which can leave you blind to routing-level issues.

screens.title: VPN versus Direct Connect monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: Although both Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect provide hybrid connectivity, their monitoring needs differ. VPNs run over the public internet, so they are prone to variable latency and packet loss; monitoring should emphasize per-tunnel health and data counters. Direct Connect is a private physical link with more predictable performance, so monitoring emphasizes physical link health, error counts, and capacity. Both need BGP monitoring because route exchange is essential. For VPNs, a TunnelState alarm typically indicates either a tunnel negotiation problem or a customer-side internet path issue; for Direct Connect, a ConnectionErrorCount increase usually implies a physical-layer problem that requires colocation or carrier involvement. Shared best practices include alerting on state changes, using minimal evaluation periods for state metrics, correlating with on-prem device logs, and sending all alerts to a single incident management stream. A key misconception is believing Direct Connect eliminates the need for deep monitoring; it reduces internet-induced variability but still requires BGP checks and error monitoring. In practice, use similar alarm philosophies for both services, tuned to each service's failure modes. VPN versus Direct Connect monitoring means use per-service monitoring tuned to failure modes: tunnel-level for vpn, link+error+bgp for direct connect, with shared alerting practices.. In practical terms, similarities, differences, and what to watch for. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Site-to-Site VPN

screens.title: Creating CloudWatch alarms (CLI example)
screens.narratorSegment: Creating CloudWatch alarms and connecting them to an SNS topic is a common operational task. The chapter gives a concrete AWS CLI example for creating an alarm on TunnelState. The example shows using the Minimum statistic, a five-minute period, and a threshold that alerts when the metric goes below 1, which indicates DOWN. When you create similar alarms for Direct Connect BGPState, use a matching pattern: short evaluation period for state flips and notification to your central incident topic. After creating the alarm, validate by checking the alarm state in CloudWatch and by triggering a test notification on your SNS topic. A misconception to avoid is setting overly sensitive thresholds that cause alert fatigue; treat state metrics with strict thresholds but tune evaluation windows and notification policies so your operations team receives clear, actionable events without noise. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › CloudWatch Alarm CLI
Code Walkthrough

CLI example

Create an alarm that fires when a VPN tunnel state goes down and notifies an SNS topic.

aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \ 
    --alarm-name "VPN_Tunnel_1_Down_Alarm" \ 
    --alarm-description "Alert when VPN Tunnel 1 goes down" \ 
    --metric-name TunnelState \ 
    --namespace AWS/VPN \ 
    --statistic Minimum \ 
    --period 300 \ 
    --threshold 1 \ 
    --comparison-operator LessThanThreshold \ 
    --dimensions Name=VpnId,Value=vpn-0abcdef1234567890 Name=TunnelIpAddress,Value=1.2.3.4 \ 
    --evaluation-periods 1 \ 
    --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:NetworkAlertsTopic \ 
    --treat-missing-data breaching
Notes
  • Replace VpnId, TunnelIpAddress, and SNS ARN with your values.
  • Use statistic Minimum and a one-evaluation period to detect state flips quickly.
  • Validate the alarm by observing CloudWatch alarm state and SNS delivery.
Key Takeaway
CLI alarms must include correct metric dimensions; test notifications and tune evaluation windows to avoid false alerts.

screens.title: Designing alarms and avoiding alert fatigue
screens.narratorSegment: Designing alarms for hybrid connectivity requires balancing sensitivity with signal quality. For binary state metrics like TunnelState and BGPState, prefer short evaluation windows and strict thresholds — you want to catch state transitions quickly. For throughput and error counters, use sensible aggregation and trend-based alerts; a single short spike may not merit an incident but a persistent increase in errors or sustained high utilization should. Avoid creating lots of single-metric alerts that flood your team; instead, group related alarms into a single incident with enriched context: include CloudWatch metric snapshots and relevant on-premises logs. Route all notifications to a central SNS topic or incident system so teams have a unified view. Regularly review alert thresholds as your traffic patterns change, and use suppression during planned maintenance windows. The misconception to avoid is setting many low-value alerts because they seemed safe; in practice they create alert fatigue and slow response to real incidents. A better approach is fewer, higher-quality alerts with clear runbooks attached. Designing alarms and avoiding alert fatigue means prefer high-signal alerts with proper aggregation, validation, and routing rather than many noisy single-metric notifications.. In practical terms, thresholds, evaluation periods, and incident routing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Designing alarms and avoiding alert fatigue

Combine alert sensitivity with context and central routing to keep your team effective.

State metrics
Short periods, strict thresholds, immediate alerts.
Throughput & errors
Use trend or sustained thresholds to avoid reacting to transient spikes.
Routing alerts

Quality over quantity: fewer, well-tuned alerts reduce fatigue and speed response.

screens.title: On-premises monitoring essentials
screens.narratorSegment: On-premises monitoring is the other half of hybrid connectivity visibility. At minimum, collect CGW interface status, C P U and memory metrics, and system logs that report IPSec negotiations and rekey events. Monitor your internal routers, firewalls, and switches that sit between your servers and the CGW, because issues in those devices can surface as cloud connectivity problems. For VPNs, collect ISP link metrics — latency, packet loss, and up/down events — since they directly affect VPN tunnel stability. For Direct Connect, collect interface error counters and physical diagnostics from your colocation provider or router. Correlate these signals with CloudWatch timestamps so you can quickly map a cloud alarm to an on-prem event. A common mistake is to silo cloud and local alerts into different systems; unify them into the same incident management feed so first responders see the full context. Finally, ensure on-prem alerts are tuned to the right thresholds and that the operations team has access to the CGW logs as part of the runbook. This setup reduces finger-pointing and lets you determine whether to engage AWS, your carrier, or the device vendor.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › On-prem Monitoring

What to collect

  • CGW interface up/down, CPU, memory, and IPSec logs.
  • BGP neighbor state and route changes from your edge routers.
  • ISP link metrics: latency, packet loss, and outages.
  • Internal device errors and interface counters for switches and firewalls.

How to use it

Correlate these local signals with CloudWatch alarms by timestamp and include them in the same incident ticket. This makes it straightforward to identify customer-side faults versus provider issues.
Common mistake
Keeping cloud and on-prem alerts in separate systems, which delays root-cause identification.

screens.title: Assessment and hands-on activity
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on activity asks you to create a CloudWatch alarm for a VPN tunnel state and a Direct Connect BGP state, then validate them alongside on-prem data sources. Start by locating your VpnId and a TunnelIpAddress, or your Direct Connect ConnectionId and VirtualInterfaceId. Create a CloudWatch alarm using the Minimum statistic with a five-minute period and the threshold set to detect a transition to DOWN. Subscribe your central SNS topic so the operations team receives notifications. Next, ensure your CGW device is forwarding interface and IPSec logs to your logging system and that BGP neighbor state changes are captured. After creating alarms, force a test event if possible, or observe real metric transitions, and confirm that the CloudWatch alarm and on-prem alert appear together in your incident queue with matching timestamps. These checks validate your monitoring and troubleshooting skills.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to monitor hybrid network links between your data center and AWS, focusing on both Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect. Reliable hybrid connectivity is critical for business continuity and application availability. We start by understanding the key CloudWatch metrics that reflect tunnel and physical link health, then we look at how on-premises monitoring fills gaps that AWS metrics cannot cover. You will see why monitoring a single metric is risky, how to design alarms that point to true failures rather than noisy spikes, and how BGP session state can block traffic even when a physical link looks healthy. As a concrete example, when a VPN tunnel metric flips between up and down you will learn why the first place to check is your customer gateway's connectivity and logs. By the end you will be able to combine CloudWatch alarms with on-premises logs and a central incident system to reduce time-to-detect and time-to-repair. Consider how these practices change if you have active/active tunnels or a dedicated Direct Connect port — the principles of redundancy, metrics, and end-to-end visibility remain the same.

These objectives will guide your work as you monitor hybrid cloud links. First, you will learn to monitor the health and performance of AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections via CloudWatch metrics such as TunnelState and TunnelDataIn/Out; being able to interpret those metrics helps you detect tunnel failures and traffic imbalance. Second, you will track AWS Direct Connect operational status and bandwidth metrics like ConnectionState and ConnectionBpsIngress/Egress, which are essential for capacity planning and diagnosing physical or routing issues. Third, you will implement logging and alerting strategies so that tunnel or BGP failures produce actionable notifications rather than noisy alerts. Finally, you will learn to monitor both AWS and on-premises sides — Customer Gateway device health, ISP links, and internal routing — to eliminate blind spots. Each skill reduces mean time to detect and repair, and together they let you build a single operational view that aligns AWS telemetry with your internal NOC processes.

To make the chapter practical, we present four measurable milestones you can validate in your environment. First, identify the TunnelState and create an alarm that triggers when a tunnel goes down; test by checking the CloudWatch metric and ensuring the SNS notification arrives. Second, observe TunnelDataIn and TunnelDataOut for traffic patterns and verify you can detect imbalances or unexpected drops. Third, configure a Direct Connect alarm for BGPState and ConnectionBpsEgress to confirm you receive alerts when routing or capacity issues occur. Fourth, demonstrate that on-premises logs — CGW interface up/down events, BGP neighbor resets, and ISP outages — are visible in your incident dashboard alongside CloudWatch alerts. Each milestone maps to a competency you can show to an operations team: detection, diagnosis, alerting, and unified visibility. These skills reduce the time you spend guessing the fault domain during an outage and lead to faster remediations.

Hybrid environments introduce two domains of visibility: the cloud provider's telemetry and your on-premises telemetry. A holistic approach recognizes that neither side alone gives full context. CloudWatch provides precise metrics for AWS-managed components — tunnel states, connection throughput, BGP session state — but it cannot see inside your customer gateway device, your internal routing, or your ISP's network. For example, a VPN tunnel metric flipping to DOWN may show the symptom, but the root cause is often an on-premises internet outage or a router interface failure. To avoid a lengthy process of elimination, proactively collect CGW logs, interface counters, C P U and memory metrics on the device, and ISP health indicators. Then correlate those with CloudWatch metrics in a single incident management workflow. Practically, this means creating alarms for key CloudWatch metrics, enriching alerts with on-prem alert data, and documenting runbooks that specify which on-prem data to check first. A common misconception is that CloudWatch alarms alone are sufficient: they are necessary but not sufficient. The core takeaway is that fast diagnosis requires correlated signals from both sides so you can distinguish provider-side faults from customer-side failures without guesswork.

AWS exposes several metrics that describe the state and throughput of Site-to-Site VPN connections. The most crucial metric for operational alerts is TunnelState: it is binary and tells you whether an individual tunnel is UP or DOWN. Because VPN connections usually have two redundant tunnels, monitoring TunnelState per tunnel avoids missing a single-tunnel failure. TunnelDataIn and TunnelDataOut measure bytes flowing through each tunnel; these are useful for spotting traffic drops, bottlenecks, or skew in active/active setups. Use TunnelData metrics to verify traffic is balanced when you expect it to be, and to detect sudden volume changes that may indicate an outage on one path. VPNConnectionState gives an aggregated view for the whole connection — helpful for dashboards but too coarse for rapid troubleshooting. Finally, newer metric names like IPSecTunnelState provide more detailed phase status for IPSec negotiations. A common misconception is treating VPNConnectionState as sufficient; it can hide single-tunnel failures. The practical rule is: alert on TunnelState for each tunnel, review TunnelData counters for performance issues, and use the aggregate metric for high-level dashboards. This combination gives both speed and context during incidents.

When a TunnelState alarm fires, follow a concise, stepwise process to isolate the fault domain quickly. First, confirm the alarm's timestamp and whether only one tunnel or both tunnels are affected. If only one tunnel is down, your first check should be the on-premises customer gateway device: review interface up/down events, C P U, memory, and the device logs for any IPSec negotiation errors. Second, check the internet path between your facility and AWS, looking for ISP outages or increased packet loss that could explain intermittent tunnel failures. Third, on the AWS side examine the tunnel's CloudWatch metrics and VPN console details to verify configuration values such as tunnel IP address and IPSec parameters. Fourth, if BGP is in use, check that session state has not been affected; a tunnel that is UP but with BGP down will still block routes. Finally, escalate to the appropriate partner — ISP, hardware vendor, or AWS Support — with correlated timestamps and logs. A common mistake is assuming the cloud side is always the problem; in practice, one tunnel failing while the redundant tunnel remains healthy usually indicates a customer-side path or device issue. This checklist reduces guesswork and speeds resolution.

Direct Connect provides a dedicated physical link between your premises and AWS. Because it bypasses the public internet, monitoring focuses on physical link health and routing. ConnectionState tells you whether the Direct Connect link is UP or DOWN — analogous to a physical port or circuit status. ConnectionBpsIngress and ConnectionBpsEgress show bandwidth utilization in bits per second and are essential for capacity planning and detecting saturation. ConnectionErrorCount counts physical layer errors; a rising error count can indicate cabling or port issues and should trigger hardware-level investigations. Critically, BGPState is the metric that reports the status of the Border Gateway Protocol session for each virtual interface. A common operational trap is assuming a UP link guarantees traffic flow; if ConnectionState is UP but BGPState is DOWN, routes are not exchanged and traffic will not be forwarded. For this reason, alerts on BGPState should be treated as high priority even when the physical connection appears healthy. Practical monitoring combines link health, bandwidth, error counts, and BGP session state into a single operational view so that you can decide quickly between hardware, configuration, or routing problems.

Although both Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect provide hybrid connectivity, their monitoring needs differ. VPNs run over the public internet, so they are prone to variable latency and packet loss; monitoring should emphasize per-tunnel health and data counters. Direct Connect is a private physical link with more predictable performance, so monitoring emphasizes physical link health, error counts, and capacity. Both need BGP monitoring because route exchange is essential. For VPNs, a TunnelState alarm typically indicates either a tunnel negotiation problem or a customer-side internet path issue; for Direct Connect, a ConnectionErrorCount increase usually implies a physical-layer problem that requires colocation or carrier involvement. Shared best practices include alerting on state changes, using minimal evaluation periods for state metrics, correlating with on-prem device logs, and sending all alerts to a single incident management stream. A key misconception is believing Direct Connect eliminates the need for deep monitoring; it reduces internet-induced variability but still requires BGP checks and error monitoring. In practice, use similar alarm philosophies for both services, tuned to each service's failure modes. VPN versus Direct Connect monitoring means use per-service monitoring tuned to failure modes: tunnel-level for vpn, link+error+bgp for direct connect, with shared alerting practices..
